papers.title: PSEN1 loss-of-function variants do not cause early-onset Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: PSEN1 variants are the most common cause of familial early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD), but it is debated whether they act through a loss- or gain-of-function. Following a recent report of a duo with EOAD carrying a predicted loss-of-function (LoF) stop-gain variant (p.K109*) in PSEN1, we sought to determine whether PSEN1 LoF variants, as a class, cause EOAD. We identified 45 carriers of PSEN1 LoF variants predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay in the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project, UK Biobank, and BioVU databases. None of these carriers had a recorded case of early-onset dementia, and 17 were older than 65 years at last follow-up with no dementia or AD reported. Re-analysis of the reported AD-associated variant p.K109* revealed a cryptic splice site predicted to produce an in-frame deletion of 5 amino acids (p.K109_L113del). These results suggest that PSEN1 variants must produce an altered PSEN1 protein product to cause EOAD, while true null LoF PSEN1 alleles do not cause EOAD.

papers.title: Monocyte-to-lymphocyte and Platelet-to-lymphocyte ratios in Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorders: systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Background: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorders (NMOSD) are a group of neuroinflammatory conditions that affect the nervous system. MLR and PLR are simple inflammatory biomarkers and are studied in many autoimmune and demyelinating diseases. In this study, we investigate the available evidence to determine whether MLR and PLR are higher in NMOSD patients than in healthy subjects. Methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies measuring levels of PLR and/or MLR in both NMOSD patients and healthy controls were conducted. Mean difference (MD) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were used to measure the difference in levels of MLR and PLR between patients and healthy subjects. Results: For MLR, the main meta-analysis yielded a pooled MD of 0.125 [-0.114; 0.363]. I2 was 83.8%. Subgroup meta-analysis of age- and sex-matched studies, demonstrated a pooled MD of 0.066 [0.012; 0.12]. For PLR, meta-analysis revealed a pooled MD of 23.99 [6.03; 41.96]. I2 was 82.3%. Subgroup analysis for age- and sex-matched studies for PLR, showed a pooled MD of 14 [-19.68; 47.68]. Conclusion: The main analysis suggests that MLR is not higher in NMOSD patients than in healthy controls. However, subgroup analysis of age- and sex-matched studies and leave-one-out analysis excluding the outlier study showed a statistically significant MLR increase in patients. PLR was found to exhibit a modest increase in NMOSD patients compared with healthy controls. Nonetheless, subgroup analysis of age- and sex-matched studies showed a statistically non-significant increase. Results should be interpreted cautiously. The available evidence is inconsistent and further research is needed.

papers.title: Age and body-mass index account for part of the sex differences in cerebral venous thrombosis
papers.abstract: Background. Women with cerebral venous thrombosis are younger than men and more often present with headache, but the cohorts reporting these differences did not account for age or body-mass index, both of which differ by sex. Methods. Single-center cohort of 219 consecutive adults with confirmed cerebral venous thrombosis admitted in Zurich in 2001-2021. Presentation, imaging and laboratory findings were compared between women and men, and every difference was re-estimated at equal age and body-mass index. Secondary analyses compared functional outcome, residual symptoms and return to work by sex, with an audit of incomplete follow-up. Results. Women (132, 60.3%) were younger (47.3 versus 54.9 years) and had a lower body-mass index (25.9 versus 27.8 kg/m2) than men. Headache (72.0% versus 57.5%) and cortical vein thrombosis (14.4% versus 5.7%) were more frequent in women, but neither association persisted after adjustment (odds ratios, 1.17 [95% CI, 0.54-2.54] and 2.05 [95% CI, 0.59-7.06]). Higher platelet counts (+56 x 109/L [95% CI, 26-86]) and elevated acute-phase markers without documented infection (59.1% versus 33.3%; odds ratio, 2.91 [95% CI, 1.44-5.87]) persisted after adjustment for age, body-mass index and calendar period. Among assessed patients (38% at 6 months), functional independence (86.3% versus 87.5%), residual headache, return to work and recanalization did not differ by sex. Conclusions. At equal age and body-mass index, the female excess of headache and cortical vein involvement was no longer apparent, whereas a higher platelet count and a non-specific acute-phase response remained. Neither translated into a difference in outcome among assessed patients.

papers.title: DxToniaNet: A Neural Network for Estimating the Severity of Leg Dystonia in Children with Cerebral Palsy
papers.abstract: Importance: Leg dystonia affects 50-80% of children with cerebral palsy (CP), but severity assessment remains subjective and time-consuming. Objective tools are urgently needed to quantify leg dystonia severity in clinical care and clinical trials. Objective: To develop and validate a deep neural network (DxToniaNet) for leg dystonia severity estimation using 2D clinical video recordings. Design, Setting, and Participants: We retrospectively analyzed video recordings of 298 children with cerebral palsy undergoing a seated hand open-close task as part of routine clinical care (Center 1: 193 videos, 720p/30fps; Center 2: 105 videos, 4K/60fps). Videos were rated for leg dystonia severity by a group of 7 experts using the Global Dystonia Rating Scale (GDRS) leg subscore (range 0-40) which has a minimum clinically important difference (MCID) of 4 points. Videos displaying leg dystonia (median expert GDRS score [≥]1) were used to develop and test a machine learning model (DxToniaNet) for estimating leg dystonia severity. Open-source software (OpenPose) estimated bilateral knee, ankle, and toe coordinates, normalized for height and camera positioning, and 69 variance and amplitude features were calculated based on established expert-cited features of leg dystonia. A neural network, DxToniaNet, was developed, trained and validated using 5-fold cross-validation on Center 1 videos before final testing on independent Center 2 videos. Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s): Mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and accuracy in differentiating between videos with clinically meaningful differences in GDRS scores were calculated relative to experts' median GDRS scores. Results: When estimating experts' leg GDRS scores in testing data, the proposed machine learning (ML) model yielded a MAE of 1.71 {+/-} 1.68 and RMSE of 2.21 {+/-} 0.34 (significantly less than the GDRS MCID of 4), and 90-94% accuracy in differentiating between videos with greater than a 4-point difference in the GDRS. Conclusions and Relevance: We have demonstrated that DxToniaNet can accurately estimate leg dystonia severity compared to experts' assessments with a small (clinically insignificant) error margin. Our methodology supports generalizability since DxToniaNet was developed and tested using independent videos datasets from different centers, recorded under different conditions. In the future, DxToniaNet may help facilitate standardized leg dystonia severity estimation in clinical care and clinical trials.

papers.title: Unraveling the Lifespan Trajectory of White Matter Hypointensity on T1-weighted MR Images and Clinical Application in Various Brain Disorders
papers.abstract: White matter hypointensity on T1-weighted MRI (T1-WMHypo), a putative marker of white matter pathophysiological changes, has been less systematically investigated than the widely studied T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (T2-FLAIR) hyperintensity lesions. Here, we built the lifespan normative reference and assessed the clinical significance of T1-WMHypo across various brain disorders using a large multicenter dataset. We first established lifespan normative reference for T1-WMHypo volume by 34,148 healthy individuals (aged 4-85 years). Then, in 7,587 patients across 21 neurological and psychiatric disorders, normative reference-derived deviations revealed disease-specific patterns, with marked deviations in neurological diseases. Deviations of T1-WMHypo volume contributed to differential diagnosis, larger deviations correlated with brain atrophy, cognitive impairment, and poorer outcomes in various brain disorders. Elevated burden of T1-WMHypo volume predicted poor medication response in Parkinson's disease and accelerated disability progression in multiple sclerosis. These associations persisted after adjusting for conventional T2-FLAIR hyperintensity lesions. T1-WMHypo deviations provide an individualized marker of white matter pathophysiological changes, offering novel insights for precision medicine across development, aging and brain disorders.

papers.title: Histological characteristics of the quadriceps muscle and their associations with gait in older adults
papers.abstract: Background/objective: There is a paucity of data about muscle morphology in aging adults. We quantified histologic features of the quadriceps muscle and examined their associations with gait function and physical activity in community-dwelling older adults. Methods: Participants were from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Postmortem sections of the quadriceps muscles were examined by immunohistochemistry using antibodies against myosin heavy chain, and histological characteristics of the quadriceps muscles were derived through images quantifications and segmentations. In addition, brain sections were assessed for collection of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias pathologies. Before death, participants' physical activity was objectively measured through wearing an accelerometer sensor for 10 days, and gait function was quantified by walking 8 feet and turning 360o twice. Linear regressions and compositional analyses were used for analyzing data. Results: Postmortem quadriceps was examined in 236 decedents (mean age at death was 91.7 years (SD=6.0), and 71.6% (n=169) were females. On average, 44.7% (SD=19.5) of the muscle fibers were type I and 54.2% (SD=19.4) were type II, and 40.6% (SD=13.0) and 21.9% (12.9) of the quadriceps muscle area were composed of type I and II muscle fibers, respectively. In compositional analyses, male sex (estimate=0.303, SE=0.126, p=0.016) and more physical activity (estimate=0.118, SE=0.059, p=0.045) were associated with larger quadriceps muscle areas with type II muscle fibers, which were related to better gait (estimate=-0.049, SE=0.021, p=0.021). Quadriceps muscle composition explained an additional 3.2% of gait's variance beyond the 5.8% variance explained by Alzheimer's disease and related dementias brain pathologies. Conclusion: Quadriceps muscles having larger areas with type II muscle fibers were associated with more physical activity and better gait function in aging adults. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying these associations are critical for developing new therapies.

papers.title: Robust Feature Engineering Techniques for Designing Efficient Motor Imagery-Based Systems Using Multidomain Electroencephalography
papers.abstract: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have potential applications in neurorehabilitation; however, the high dimensionality and complexity of electroencephalography (EEG) signals present challenges for accurate classification. This study aimed to improve the classification of motor and motor imagery activities using multidomain feature engineering and feature selection on the MILimbEEG dataset. Time-domain, frequency-domain, and wavelet-based features were extracted from 16-channel EEG signals, yielding 416 features. Maximum relevance minimum redundancy (MRMR) was then applied to select the four most informative and minimally redundant features. These features were used to train support vector machine (SVM), K-nearest neighbors (KNN), Naive Bayes, and decision tree classifiers, with performance evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation based on testing accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The Gaussian-kernel SVM achieved the highest testing accuracies of 92.50% for motor activities and 95.48% for motor imagery activities. For the highest-performing motor imagery classification, precision, recall, and F1-score were 86.97%, 88.33%, and 87.04%, respectively. These findings demonstrate that reducing 416 multidomain EEG features to four discriminative features using MRMR can maintain strong classification performance. The proposed feature-engineering framework may support the development of computationally efficient EEG-based BCI systems for neurorehabilitation applications.

papers.title: A Multi-Cohort nnU-Net for White Matter Hyperintensity Segmentation Across 2D and 3D FLAIR Acquisitions
papers.abstract: Background White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are increasingly pooled across aging, cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), and dementia cohorts that differ in both disease composition and FLAIR acquisition. Most automated segmentation tools were developed within a narrower range of populations or protocols, and few have been tested for whether segmentation accuracy and error remain consistent across conventional 2D and isotropic 3D FLAIR, or whether the choice of algorithm alters downstream clinical associations. Methods We developed a single nnU-Net model, taking FLAIR and T1-weighted images as inputs, using 460 2D and 3D FLAIR scans from a neurodegenerative cohort (Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, ADNI), a CSVD-enriched cohort with same-visit paired 2D and 3D FLAIR (Washington University White Matter Ischemic-Hypoxia study, WWISH), and a population-based sample (UK Biobank), holding out 92 scans from 66 participants at the participant-level as an internal test set. We further evaluated the model in an independent ADNI3 3D FLAIR set (n = 25), benchmarking voxel-wise overlap (Dice), volumetric agreement, and lesion-level detection against SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and FreeSurfer WMH-SynthSeg, and compared acquisition-specific volume bias in participants with paired 2D and 3D FLAIR. We then compared how WMH volumes from each method predicted incident dementia in cognitively unimpaired adults from ADNI and the Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center (n = 1,174; 42 incident cases). Results In the internal test set, the model achieved a mean Dice of 0.73 (SD 0.10), compared with 0.50, 0.57, and 0.29 for SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and WMH-SynthSeg (all FDR-adjusted p < 0.001). Dice was similar on 2D and 3D FLAIR (0.75 vs. 0.71). In WWISH participants imaged with both acquisitions, mean volume bias differed between 2D and 3D scans by 1.8 mL for the model versus 4.7-9.9 mL for the comparators. Advantages were largest in low-burden scans (<5 mL; Dice 0.66 vs. 0.19-0.54) and for lesions of [≤]100 voxels (detection 77-87% vs. 14-63%). In ADNI3, the model retained a mean Dice of 0.70 (SD 0.14) without retraining and exceeded all comparators (FDR-adjusted p [≤] 0.002). Model-derived WMH volume was associated with incident dementia beyond clinical covariates (OR per SD 1.40, 95% CI 1.11-1.77; likelihood-ratio p = 0.009; cross-validated AUC 0.71 vs. 0.68), whereas comparator-derived volumes did not significantly improve model fit. Conclusions Training a single model across disease contexts and FLAIR acquisitions yielded WMH segmentation that was similarly accurate on 2D and 3D FLAIR, sensitive to low-burden disease, transferable to an unseen protocol, and clinically informative, supporting its use in multi-cohort, mixed-etiology studies.

papers.title: Sub-Threshold Stochastic Vibration Improves Fingertip Tactile Sensitivity in Stroke Survivors and Healthy Adults, with Source-Localized EEG Evidence for Cortical Network Reorganization in Healthy Adults
papers.abstract: Cutaneous sensation is vital for daily function and safety, yet it commonly declines with ageing and after neurological injury, with stroke survivors particularly affected. This study investigates whether sub-threshold stochastic (random) vibrations can enhance light-touch (cutaneous) sensation in healthy adults and stroke survivors and characterizes the associated changes in cortical functional connectivity (FC). Nineteen healthy participants and five stroke survivors took part. A custom device delivered sinusoidal and stochastic vibrations to the volar surface of the right middle fingertip. For each participant we first determined the detection threshold for stochastic vibration alone, then the threshold for a 30 Hz sinusoidal vibration, and then the threshold for that sinusoidal vibration combined with imperceptible stochastic noise fixed at 80% of the stochastic threshold; in ten healthy participants a super-threshold combination (120% of the stochastic threshold) was also tested. High-density (64-channel) electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded throughout for the healthy participants. Adding sub- threshold stochastic noise lowered the sinusoidal detection threshold in every participant tested and produced consistent reductions in all five stroke survivors; expressed as gains in sensitivity, individual improvements reached up to 19 times in healthy participants and up to 4 times in stroke survivors. Source- localized EEG showed that sub-threshold stochastic vibration significantly increased FC, most extensively in the alpha band, with prominent involvement of frontal regions (superior and rostral middle frontal cortices and anterior cingulate; cluster- based permutation p < 0.05), consistent with a noise-driven modulation of sensory and attentional networks. Super-threshold noise produced weaker, predominantly beta-band changes, in line with signal masking rather than resonance. These findings indicate that sub-threshold stochastic vibration lowers light-touch detection thresholds and reorganizes cortical connectivity in both healthy and stroke populations, and they support prioritizing cutaneous sensation in stochastic-resonance based neurorehabilitation for stroke survivors.

papers.title: Longitudinal Cerebrospinal Fluid Biomarker Changes Following Shunt Surgery in Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus - Insights from the Gothenburg POiNT study
papers.abstract: Background The underlying pathophysiology of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is incompletely understood and reliable predictors of shunt response are lacking. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers may provide insights into disease mechanisms and help identify patients most likely to benefit from surgery. The aim of this study was to explore CSF biomarker dynamics following shunt surgery and their relationship with clinical outcome. Methods The POiNT (Prediction of Outcome in iNPH) was a prospective longitudinal study. One hundred and thirty-five patients with iNPH underwent standardized clinical assessment and lumbar CSF sampling 3.6 (SD 2.1) months before and 5.7 months (SD 2.4) after shunt surgery. CSF was analyzed for biomarkers of astrogliosis, axonal injury, amyloid, and tau pathology, and synaptic dysfunction. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the iNPH scale. Associations between baseline biomarker levels, postoperative biomarker changes, and clinical outcomes were evaluated using adjusted correlation and regression analyses. Results In total, 69% (n=93) improved after shunt surgery. Substantial postoperative increases were observed for most CSF biomarkers: The largest relative increases were seen for growth-associated protein 43 (GAP43) (2.92-fold change), followed by Phosphorylated tau (2.65-fold change), Neurogranin and total-tau (both 2.29-fold change) as well as A{beta}40 (1.93-fold change), and A{beta}42 (1.76-fold change) (all p<0.001). In adjusted analyses, postoperative change in several biomarker levels were associated with degree of clinical improvement. However, baseline biomarker levels generally showed limited predictive value. Lower baseline monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP1) levels were associated with greater odds of overall clinical improvement but had a modest predictive performance (AUC 0.67). No baseline biomarker demonstrated strong discrimination of treatment response. Conclusion Shunt surgery was associated with substantial changes in CSF biomarker concentrations, several of which correlated with the degree of clinical improvement. Although baseline levels did not predict clinical outcome, the observed biomarker changes may reflect biological responses to treatment, altered CSF dynamics, or both .iNPH. Future studies examining these processes relating to disease reversibility might help elucidate pathophysiological mechanisms in iNPH.

papers.title: Atrophy-related inflammation CSF markers predict clinical progression in genetic frontotemporal dementia
papers.abstract: Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognised as a key contributor to frontotemporal dementia (FTD) pathophysiology, yet how inflammatory processes relate to neurodegeneration and clinical progression remains poorly defined. This study aimed to identify a multivariate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inflammatory signature covarying with brain atrophy, and to determine its relevance to clinical and cognitive outcomes in genetic FTD. We recruited 234 participants (non-carrier controls n=78, presymptomatic carriers n=115, symptomatic carriers n=41) with CSF, MRI, and clinical (CDR (r) + NACC FTLD sum of boxes [CDR-SB]) and executive (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Revised Digit Symbol Substitution Task [DSST] assessments. A regularised canonical correlation analysis (rCCA) was used to derive a shared protein-brain covariance axis. Participants were followed annually for up to 8.6 years (CDR-SB) and 11.5 years (DSST), and linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate individual rates of clinical progression (CDR slope) and executive decline (DSST slope). The predictive value of the inflammation- and MRI-based profiles for cross-sectional CDR-SB, CDR slope, DSST and DSST slope were tested in linear models. Due to floor effects and violations of parametric assumptions, Bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence intervals (CI) and bootstrap CIs (95%, 5000 replicates) were utilised as the primary inferential criterion in the 2nd-level linear models; effects were considered non-significant if the 95% BCa CI crossed zero. The rCCA identified a robust inflammation-brain axis (r=0.89, p<0.001), driven by CXCL9, FLT3L, CCL3, and frontotemporal-insular atrophy pattern. In symptomatic carriers, the MRI canonical variate was associated with CDR-SB (beta=3.80, CI: [0.64, 6.20]) at baseline, whereas the inflammatory protein canonical variate was predictive of CDR-SB slope (beta=0.24, CI: [0.02, 0.46]). Whereas both MRI (beta= -7.27, CI:[-14.20, -1.00]) and protein (beta= -7.83, CI:[-14.00, -2.16]) canonical variates were linked to DSST cross-sectionally, but not longitudinally. No significant associations were found in pre-symptomatic carriers or non-carrier controls. A data-driven CSF inflammatory signature, covarying with frontotemporal-insular atrophy, tracks with clinical severity and cognitive impairment in people with genetic FTD, highlighting inflammation as a candidate therapeutic target and progression biomarker in the earliest clinically manifest stages of disease.

papers.title: Cross-cohort validation of EEG biomarkers using a pre-registered three-criterion framework: a demonstration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
papers.abstract: Background. Despite decades of EEG biomarker development for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), no candidate has progressed to clinical deployment, partly because cross-cohort validation is rare. We aimed to develop and demonstrate a pre-registered three-criterion screening framework to identify which candidate EEG features show the combined properties required for biomarker translation: cross-sectional discrimination, within-subject reliability, and cross-cohort effect consistency. Methods. We pre-registered a validation framework adapted from FDA-NIH BEST principles and applied it to 18 EEG features across three independent cohorts: EEGET-ALS (six ALS patients, 170 healthy controls; home recordings over 17 days), UCL/Penn State (eight ALS patients; clinic recordings over 1-2 months), and a healthy adult test-retest reference (60 participants, three sessions over one month). Features were required to meet three pre-registered criteria: (1) cross-sectional discrimination (Cohen's d > 0.5), (2) within-subject reliability (ICC(3,1) > 0.6 in both ALS cohorts independently), and (3) cross-cohort effect direction consistency. Cross-cohort permutation testing (1000 iterations) and subject-level bootstrap resampling (500 iterations) were applied to assess robustness. Results. Three features met all three pre-registered criteria: gamma power, theta power, and spectral entropy. Cross-cohort permutation testing showed that no permutation, out of 1000, produced any feature in the three-cohort reliability intersection (Monte Carlo p = 0.001). Bootstrap resampling indicated that the composition of the selected set was sensitive to sample composition (median count 1, 95% CI [0, 4]), with gamma power (67% inclusion), spectral entropy (43%), and theta power (32%) the most stable features at a relaxed reliability threshold (ICC > 0.5); at the primary pre-registered threshold (ICC > 0.6), the corresponding inclusion probabilities are lower (57%, 27%, and 19%, respectively). A principal methodological finding was that cross-cohort differences in feature reliability were large relative to the apparent disease-associated signal, most clearly demonstrated by relative beta power (ICC = 0.09 in a home-recorded cohort versus 0.93 in a clinic-recorded cohort); because recording protocol, hardware, setting, population, and preprocessing all differ jointly between cohorts in this dataset, this is evidence of cohort-associated variability that plausibly includes a protocol contribution, not a separately identified, isolated protocol effect. Conclusions. This study provides a pre-registered, multi-cohort EEG biomarker screening framework for ALS with explicit bootstrap-quantified uncertainty. Gamma power, spectral entropy, and theta power are identified as priority candidates for prospective validation. A recurring methodological observation is that protocol-related cohort differences appear to contribute more to cross-cohort variability than disease-related effects within this dataset; because protocol is confounded with cohort, equipment, and preprocessing, this pattern is descriptive rather than causal. The observation nonetheless has direct implications for the design of multi-site EEG biomarker studies in neural engineering.

papers.title: Tau-vulnerable medial temporal lobe connectivity drives a functional-to-synaptic cascade in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Distinct tau-vulnerable and relatively spared subregions exist within the medial temporal lobe (MTL). However, it remains unclear that how functional connectivity (FC), anchored to tau-vulnerable MTL subregions, is related to tau pathology, synaptic dysfunction, and cognitive decline across the Alzheimers disease (AD) continuum. We here probe into this with resting-state fMRI data from a discovery cohort (ADNI; N = 386; cognitively normal [CN], mild cognitive impairment [MCI], and AD; 144 with 2-year follow-up) and an independent validation cohort at local hospital (N = 100; CN, subjective cognitive decline [SCD], and MCI; 25 receiving high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation [HF-rTMS]). We first separated the MTL into subregions with high and low neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) burden based on histological atlases, and calculated the seed-based whole-brain FC for each subregion. Second, group differences were assessed using ANCOVA, and associations with amyloid-{beta} (A{beta})/tau pathology, synaptic biomarkers, and cognitive performance were examined. Third, serial mediation, cross-lagged, and longitudinal regression analyses were performed to investigate the proposed pathological sequence, with additional evidence from HF-rTMS intervention and autopsy-confirmed Braak staging. Our results showed that, with the development of AD, FC reductions were focused on the high-NFT MTL network, particularly involving the inferior temporal gyrus and precuneus. Baseline tau burden in high-NFT MTL regions was able to predict subsequent FC alterations. Interestingly, FC between the high-NFT MTL and global brain showed region-specific associations with synaptic biomarkers, including negative associations in the cerebellum and positive associations in the precentral gyrus. We also observed a divergent association between the FC and cognition or pathology at different AD stages, shifting from positive in the early stages to negative in advanced AD. Serial mediation analyses supported a pathway linking tau burden to cognitive impairment through altered high-NFT MTL connectivity in the precuneus and occipital regions and subsequent synaptic dysfunction. Cross-lagged and longitudinal analyses further confirmed the proposed temporal sequence. Furthermore, HF-rTMS-related cognitive improvements were partially associated with enhanced synaptic plasticity through changes in precuneus-high-NFT MTL connectivity. Collectively, these findings support a spatiotemporal framework linking the dysfunction of tau-vulnerable MTL network to synaptic impairment and cognitive decline, highlighting high-NFT MTL-based FC as a potential imaging marker tracking AD progression.

papers.title: LLM Embeddings Complement Theory-Driven Language Features and Cognitive Scores for APOE4 and Aβ Prediction
papers.abstract: Spontaneous language offers a scalable, noninvasive approach for identifying biological indicators of preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD). We examined prediction of APOE4 carrier status and cerebral amyloid-beta burden using Cookie Theft picture descriptions from two cohorts of Hebrew- and English-speaking participants (IRAP, N=134; WRAP, N=1,541). Amyloid-beta burden was classified using lowest-quartile, median, and highest-quartile cutoffs, capturing accumulation below conventional amyloid-positivity thresholds. We compared embeddings from pretrained large language models (LLMs) with standard cognitive test scores, reflecting conventional clinical assessment, and theory-driven linguistic features, reflecting traditional language analysis. Embedding-based models achieved the highest F1 scores among constituent models in five of eight tasks involving APOE4 status and global amyloid-beta burden. High prediction disagreement suggested complementary signals across approaches. An any-positive ensemble significantly outperformed every constituent model and a prior-informed random baseline across all eight tasks, and significantly outperformed all constituent models in 21 of 24 regional amyloid-beta tasks. These findings highlight the complementarity of LLM-based, theory-driven, and cognitive measures for predicting AD-related genetic risk and amyloid pathology, and support further investigation of their potential for early screening approaches.

papers.title: Higher platelet counts are associated with migraine risk across three cohorts among more than 21,000 cases
papers.abstract: ObjectiveWe assessed potential associations between migraine and complete blood cell count (CBC) data in three large population-based studies. BackgroundPlatelets are thought to be involved in migraine pathology through increased activation during an attack. Migraine attacks are often treated with NSAIDs that inhibit platelets, or triptans that target serotonin receptors, with serotonin being most highly expressed in circulation within platelet granules. However, the exact role of platelets in migraine remains unclear. MethodsThe UK BioBank (UKBB) has CBC data available from baseline blood samples and migraine diagnoses were obtained through self-report and electronic health records. CBC and migraine data from the 1999-2000, 2001-2002, and 2003-2004 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) study were obtained during single exam visits. CBCs were obtained from Framingham Heart Study (FHS) participants. Migraine history was assessed through clinical diagnostic impressions. The UKBB sample (18,919 cases (4,580 incident); 448,339 controls) was the primary discovery cohort for CBCs, with replication meta-analysis done in NHANES (1,887 cases; 7,242 controls) and FHS (395 cases (229 incident); 3,172 controls). Our primary model adjusted for age and sex, with secondary analysis adjusting for additional factors. Sex-stratified, sex-interaction and ancestry-stratified (UKBB only) analyses were also performed. ResultsMigraine was associated with platelet count (PLT) in the UKBB (OR=1.058, 95% CI [1.043,1.073], p=2.09E-14) and was replicated in the NHANES-FHS meta-analysis (OR=1.074, 95% CI [1.025,1.126], p=0.003). PLT also drove multiple significant signals of PLT-involved CBC ratios. While neutrophil counts and hemoglobin were associated with migraine in UKBB, these did not replicate in FHS-NHANES meta-analysis. ConclusionHigher platelet count is associated with an increased likelihood of migraine. Further studies with longitudinal assessments of CBCs and migraine attacks are needed to further understand the role of platelets in the onset of migraine attacks.

papers.title: Peripheral Blood NADP(H) Redox Metabolism in Alzheimers Disease and Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis Where Feasible
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe reduced and oxidized forms of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH/NADP{square}) connect cellular reducing power with the glutathione and thioredoxin systems. Peripheral alterations in this network may reflect systemic redox dysregulation in Alzheimers disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI), but the evidence has not been quantitatively synthesized. ObjectiveTo systematically evaluate peripheral-blood NADP(H) redox metabolism and related enzymes in AD and MCI and to perform meta-analyses when the available data were sufficiently comparable. MethodsPubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 6 November 2026. Eligible observational studies compared patients with AD or MCI with cognitively unimpaired controls and reported NADPH, NADP{square}, the NADPH/NADP{square} ratio, or NADPH-related enzymes, including glutathione reductase (GR), glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), and thioredoxin reductase (TRXR). Continuous outcomes were converted to Hedges g. Random-effects models used restricted maximum likelihood estimation and modified Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals. ResultsOf 2,686 records identified, 1,781 remained after deduplication and 13 studies were included. No study directly reported peripheral NADPH, NADP{square}, or the NADPH/NADP{square} ratio. The pooled effect for erythrocyte GR in AD was g=-1.05 (95% CI -2.73 to 0.63; I2=95.0%; five studies); for erythrocyte GR in MCI, g=-0.15 (95% CI -8.68 to 8.38; I2=95.0%; two studies); for whole-blood/plasma GR in AD, g=-0.03 (95% CI -4.37 to 4.30; I2=97.1%; three studies); and for erythrocyte G6PD in AD, g=-0.66 (95% CI -17.36 to 16.03; I2=96.4%; two studies). Leave-one-out analyses did not materially alter the interpretation of the erythrocyte GR synthesis. ConclusionsAD and MCI may be accompanied by remodeling of peripheral NADP(H)-related enzyme networks, but the direction and magnitude of effects are inconsistent across studies. Direct measurement of NADPH, NADP{square}, and their ratio remains the most important evidence gap. Future prospective studies should standardize specimen type, pre-analytical handling, and analytical platforms and should account for disease stage, treatment exposure, and metabolic comorbidity.

papers.title: Serum brain-derived tau distinguishes acute neurotrauma diagnoses
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) are two common forms of neurotrauma that can present with overlapping clinical features, complicating early diagnosis and management particularly in acute and mixed-trauma settings.1-3 Accurate and rapid biological differentiation remains an unmet need.4 We hypothesized that brain-derived tau (BD-tau), an ultrasensitive blood-based biomarker preferentially selective for tau protein originating from the brain, would distinguish TBI from SCI. In a multi-cohort assessment of 342 patients admitted to the neuro-intensive care unit (285 with TBI, 57 with SCI), and 22 controls, baseline serum BD-tau concentrations were markedly elevated in TBI compared with SCI, discriminating between the two populations with high accuracy (area under the curve [AUC]=0.91, 95%CI 0.87-0.96). In paired serum-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples, serum BD-tau significantly outperformed CSF BD-tau for injury-type discrimination (AUC=0.95, 95%CI 0.89-0.99 vs. 0.80, 95%CI 0.71-0.89). Baseline serum BD-tau also showed superior discrimination of TBI from SCI compared with established blood biomarkers of neurotrauma, including neurofilament light chain, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (AUC=0.82, 95%CI 0.76-0.88; vs. 0.53, 95%CI 0.43-0.63; 0.67, 95%CI 0.58-0.76; 0.71, 95%CI 0.64-0.79; all DeLong p<0.001). Longitudinally, serum BD-tau remained persistently elevated in TBI, but not SCI, for up to 144 hours post-injury, with distinct temporal trajectories between injury types. Together, these findings indicate that serum BD-tau enables rapid and minimally invasive differentiation of TBI from SCI and may support early clinical decision-making, triage, and enrollment into injury-specific therapeutic trials, highlighting the potential of circulating biomarkers to improve precision diagnostics in acute neurotrauma care.

papers.title: Scalp EEG seizure warning in children under a pre-specified, locked evaluation: confound audit, structured chance levels and a negative result
papers.abstract: Reported performance of scalp electroencephalographic (EEG) seizure pre-diction is often inflated by lenient evaluation and by the vigilance-state, clock-time and admission-trend structure of monitoring data. We asked how much short-horizon warning survives a pre-specified, locked evaluation. Continuous video-EEG from 21 monitored children (1315 h) formed the development cohort. A statistical-process-control warning method, evaluated under a written protocol, detected 44% of evaluable seizures at 0.48 false alarms per hour, no better than a random predictor (51%, p = 0.86); its statistic moved three times more with vigilance state than with seizure approach. We re-designed it as a state-conditioned, directional scheme on seven global EEG features, froze it with a hash-recorded configuration and time-stamped pre-specification, and estimated its performance by nested leave-one-patient-out cross-validation: 15 of 45 seizures (33%) at 0.47 false alarms per hour, above analytic (21%, p = 0.034) and permutation chance, but a predictor using only clock time, vigilance state and days since admission reproduced most of this, and the signal was confined to the last 30 min. Applied once to two validation cohorts (a second batch from the same unit and the public CHB-MIT database; 101 evaluable seizures), the frozen scheme detected 19 seizures (19%) at 0.60 false alarms per hour against 26% chance (p = 0.96); no secondary endpoint was met, and with the child as the unit of analysis no cohort was above chance. Scalp-EEG warning should be evaluated under pre-specified rules against structured chance levels; the frozen scheme and framework are offered as a reference.

papers.title: Reduced serum carboxymethyllysine is independently associated with Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTIONAdvanced glycation end products accumulate in Alzheimers disease (AD) brain, but the clinical significance of circulating N{varepsilon}-(carboxymethyl)lysine (CML) remains uncertain. We evaluated serum CML as a complementary peripheral biomarker of AD. METHODSThis observational case-control study enrolled 101 patients with clinically diagnosed AD and 91 healthy controls. Serum CML was quantified in 191 participants. Multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic analyses assessed association and discrimination. A randomly selected subcohort underwent ultrasensitive measurement of amyloid-, tau-, glial-, and neuroaxonal-related biomarkers. RESULTSSerum CML was lower in AD than controls (median 15.26 versus 23.72 ng/mL; P<0.001). In a complete-case model (n=178), each 1-ng/mL increase was associated with lower odds of AD (adjusted odds ratio 0.727, 95% confidence interval 0.656-0.804). CML alone yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.883. Five-fold cross-validation yielded AUCs of 0.727 for a clinical model and 0.911 after adding CML. In the biomarker subcohort, AD showed lower A{beta}42/A{beta}40 and higher p-tau217; exploratory CML plus p-tau217 discrimination reached an AUC of 0.966 (n=60). DISCUSSIONReduced serum CML was independently associated with clinically diagnosed AD and may reflect a systemic glycoxidative dimension complementary to canonical biomarkers. Its biological origins and clinical value require external, longitudinal, and biomarker-defined validation.

papers.title: The effect of carotid atherosclerosis and revascularization on cognition and dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundCarotid artery atherosclerosis may accelerate cognitive decline and increase dementia risk, but evidence is fragmented and inconsistent, and benefit of revascularization on cognitive outcomes uncertain. MethodsWe systematically searched Medline, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Central Register, and Google Scholar for articles published until 11 November 2024, reporting change in cognition or dementia incidence in relation to carotid artery intima-media thickness, plaque, stenosis, and revascularization procedures. We excluded studies that investigated people with dementia, lacked a reference group, or had post-intervention follow-up <30 days. We additionally included new data from the Rotterdam Study, and results from the recent CREST-2 trial. Two independent reviewers extracted study data. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed if data allowed. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, Cochrane Risk of Bias, and ROBINS-I. ResultsOf 5592 records identified, 97 studies were eligible, including 43 observational studies (N=100,326) and 54 intervention studies (N=15788, 6 randomized controlled trials). In observational studies, mostly among stroke-free individuals, intima-media thickness was associated with higher dementia risk (hazard ratio per 1-SD increase: 1.07, 95%CI 1.01-1.13; I2=24.8%; 5 studies), as was presence of 50-100% asymptomatic steno-occlusive disease (hazard ratio: 1.48, 95%CI 1.06-2.07; I2=0.0%, 3 studies). Cognitive outcomes were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis, but 11/20 observational studies reported a significant association between carotid atherosclerosis and global cognition. In non-randomized intervention studies, carotid revascularization improved global cognition (standardized mean difference: 0.73, 95%CI 0.37-1.09; I2=89.8%), but all studies were at high risk of bias, and heterogeneity was only partially explained by intervention type and study characteristics in meta-regression. Suggested benefit of stenting on cognition among Chinese patients (Standardized effect: 0.86 [0.57-1.16], 197 patients; and 1.09 [0.64-1.53], 90 patients, 2 trials) was not observed in the larger CREST-2 trial (Standardized effect: 0.03 [-0.09 to 0.15] and 0.02 [-0.09 to 0.14]), nor in post-hoc analyses of cognition in the ACAS trial and long-term dementia risk in ACST-1 (HR: 0.98 [0.75-1.28]). ConclusionsCarotid atherosclerosis is associated with increased risk of dementia. Current evidence does not support carotid revascularization for prevention of cognitive decline or dementia.

papers.title: A Multicenter Retrospective Study on the Safety and Efficacy of the Surpass Evolve Flow Diverter System for the Treatment of Intracranial Aneurysms
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the safety and efficacy of the Surpass Evolve flow diverter system for the treatment of intracranial aneurysms across three medical centers. MethodsA retrospective review was conducted on patients with intracranial aneurysms treated with the Surpass Evolve FDS between March 2023 and May 2024 at three participating centers. Primary outcome measures included the rate of complete aneurysm occlusion (Raymond-Roy class 1) and the incidence of periprocedural major stroke and mortality. Secondary outcomes encompassed follow-up modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores, imaging assessment results, and complication rates. ResultsA total of 132 patients (132 aneurysms) were included. The median age was 60.0 years (IQR 52.5-69.0), and 80 patients (66.6%) were female. The complete occlusion rate was 73.3% (88/120). The rate of major stroke was 2.3%, with no procedure-related mortality. At follow-up, 96.9% of patients had an mRS score of 0-2. Multivariate analysis identified non-use of an intraprocedural IIb/IIIa inhibitor and the absence of a branch arising from the aneurysm as independent predictors of complete occlusion. ConclusionIn this real-world, multicenter, retrospective study, the treatment of intracranial aneurysms with the Surpass Evolve FDS was associated with a high rate of complete occlusion and a favorable safety profile. Our findings indicate that complete occlusion was independently predicted by two key factors: periprocedural avoidance of IIb/IIIa inhibitors and a favorable aneurysm morphology without incorporated branches.

papers.title: Feasibility of Vibrotactile P50 Sensory-Gating Assessment Using Portable EEG
papers.abstract: Sensory gating (SG), most commonly quantified using the auditory P50 event-related potential elicited by a paired "double-click" paradigm, is a well-established biomarker of early sensory inhibition that reflects the brains ability to suppress responses to repetitive sensory input. Although auditory SG paradigms have been widely used in both research and clinical settings, they impose an unavoidable auditory load and are generally limited to controlled laboratory environments, reducing their suitability for ecological monitoring and applications in which auditory resources must remain available. This study evaluated the feasibility of a portable vibrotactile sensory-gating system designed to assess inhibitory processing without engaging the auditory or visual modalities. Fifteen healthy adult participants completed both auditory and vibrotactile paired-stimulus conditions using a within-subject experimental design. Vibrotactile stimuli were delivered through transducers positioned on the volar surface of the forearm while electroencephalographic (EEG) activity was recorded using a 32-channel Emotiv EPOC Flex system. Event-related responses were extracted and analyzed using conventional sensory-gating metrics to enable direct comparison between modalities. Vibrotactile stimulation elicited time-locked P50 responses with attenuation of S2 relative to S1. Mean S2/S1 ratios were 0.521 {+/-} 0.041 for the auditory condition and 0.524 {+/-} 0.064 for the vibrotactile condition. The paired difference was 0.0029 (95% CI, -0.0221 to 0.0279), t(14) = 0.249, p = 0.807, dz = 0.064. No statistically significant difference was detected between modalities in this sample. These group-level findings support further evaluation of portable vibrotactile P50 measurement.

papers.title: Donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine and progression to memantine add-on therapy in Alzheimer's disease: a nationwide cohort study emulating a target trial in the Brazilian Unified Health System
papers.abstract: BackgroundDonepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine are dispensed free of charge to people with mild to moderate Alzheimers disease in the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS), but their comparative long-term effectiveness in routine care is unknown. Under the national clinical protocol, memantine is added to a cholinesterase inhibitor (ChEI) when the disease reaches the moderate stage, so memantine add-on can serve as a marker of clinical progression. MethodsNationwide new-user cohort study emulating a target trial in which adults with Alzheimers disease eligible for a ChEI would be randomly assigned to start donepezil, galantamine or rivastigmine and followed for memantine add-on. We used outpatient medication dispensing authorizations (APAC records of the Outpatient Information System, SIA/SUS) from all 27 federative units, January 2018 to December 2025. We included patients who started a single ChEI between October 2019, after memantine was first recorded nationally, and December 2025, after at least 12 months without anti-dementia dispensing. The outcome was the first memantine dispensing after the index month. Follow-up ended at add-on, recorded death, loss to follow-up (more than 3 observed months without dispensing) or end of data. Deaths were rarely recorded and were treated as censoring. One pseudonymized health card number shared by many patients was excluded, and follow-up ended earlier in the two affected states. We estimated the risk of add-on at 12 to 48 months had all patients started each drug and remained under observation, using stabilized inverse probability of treatment and censoring weights, with 95% confidence intervals (CI) from 200 bootstrap replicates. The analysis assumed no unmeasured confounding or informative censoring given the measured covariates. ResultsThe cohort included 142 758 new users (donepezil 74 165; galantamine 30 691; rivastigmine 37 902; mean age 77.3 years; 63.0% women), followed for a median of 14 months; 9 812 memantine add-on events occurred. After weighting, all standardized mean differences were below 0.05. The 24-month weighted cumulative incidence of memantine add-on was 9.7% (95% CI 9.4-10.0) with donepezil, 9.0% (8.6-9.4) with galantamine and 5.6% (5.3- 5.9) with rivastigmine. Compared with donepezil, the 24-month risk difference was -0.7 percentage points (pp) (-1.1 to -0.3) for galantamine and -4.1 pp (-4.5 to -3.7) for rivastigmine (risk ratio 0.58, 0.55-0.61). Estimates were stable across sensitivity analyses, including a composite outcome that counted unrecorded deaths and dropouts as events (24month risk difference -4.1 pp, -4.8 to -3.3) and analyses within age groups (risk ratio 0.64 below 75 years). Deaths were almost never recorded in the dispensing data (at most 0.47% of treated patients per year). ConclusionsIn routine SUS care, initiation with rivastigmine, mostly as a transdermal patch, was associated with a lower risk of memantine add-on than initiation with donepezil or galantamine. Because disease severity and death are not recorded in the dispensing data, this difference may reflect prescribing patterns or residual confounding by severity rather than slower progression; additional analyses made differential mortality a less likely explanation. It should be confirmed with linked clinical and mortality data.

papers.title: Longitudinal Investigation of Autonomic Symptoms in Biologically Confirmed (SAA+) Parkinson's Disease
papers.abstract: BackgroundAutonomic symptoms are common in Parkinsons disease (PD) and impact quality of life, with unclear relationship to motor and cognitive progression. ObjectiveCharacterize five-year progression of autonomic symptoms in early PD and their association with motor and cognitive outcomes. MethodsWe analyzed data from 874 PD participants and 252 healthy controls (HC) enrolled in Parkinsons Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). Autonomic symptoms were assessed annually over five years using Scales for Outcomes in Parkinsons disease-Autonomic dysfunction (SCOPA-AUT); affected autonomic domains were defined as domain subscore >1. Clinical measures included MDS-UPDRS and Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Generalized estimating equations evaluated longitudinal changes, adjusting for age, sex, medication, and comorbidities. ResultsAt baseline, 71% of PD participants reported >1 affected autonomic domain, increasing to 85% among 287 PD participants with 5-year follow-up; HCs reporting >1 affected autonomic domain increased from 40% of participants at baseline to 46% among 145 participants with 5-year follow-up. Gastrointestinal and urinary symptoms were most prevalent in PD. Medication use for constipation and urinary dysfunction increased over time in PD. Cardiovascular comorbidities were common and increased in prevalence in both groups. Greater baseline autonomic symptom burden predicted more rapid cognitive, but not motor decline in PD (p=0.002). ConclusionAutonomic symptoms in PD are common at disease onset, near universal after 5 years, and associated with faster cognitive, but not motor, decline, driven by those with severe symptoms. The high prevalence and impact of autonomic symptoms in early PD highlights the importance of early assessment and management of these symptoms.

papers.title: Plasma phosphorylated tau species across neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases: An ONDRI study
papers.abstract: Elevated plasma phosphorylated tau (p-tau) species are proposed as specific biomarkers of Alzheimers disease (AD) pathology but have also been reported in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Their profile across neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases, as well as their discriminatory value when combined with other plasma biomarkers, remain uncertain. We studied 551 participants (ages 40.1 to 87.1 years; 207 women), comprising 506 patients from the Ontario Neurodegenerative Disease Research Initiative (ONDRI) multi-site cohort and 45 amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) PET-negative cognitively unimpaired controls from the Brain-Eye Amyloid Memory study. Ten diagnostic groups were studied: mild cognitive impairment (MCI), AD, Parkinsons disease subdivided into cognitively unimpaired (CU), MCI, and dementia, frontotemporal dementia (FTD), cerebrovascular disease (CVD) subdivided into cognitively unimpaired (CU) and cognitively impaired (CI), ALS, and the control group. Baseline visit plasma measurements included p-tau217, p-tau181, A{beta}42/40, neurofilament light chain (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). Cross-sectional analyses compared biomarker levels as well as p-tau217-based inference of amyloid positivity status across diagnostic groups. Receiver operating characteristic-area under the curve (ROC-AUC) analyses ascertained the discriminatory capacity of these biomarkers and ratio combinations. Within the ALS group, baseline biomarker measures were also tested for association against baseline clinical features as well as longitudinal measures of neuropsychological change. P-tau217, p-tau181, GFAP, and NfL differed across groups (all P < 0.001). Compared to controls, p-tau217 was elevated in AD and ALS, p-tau181 and GFAP only in AD, and NfL in ALS and FTD. Inferred amyloid-{beta} positivity was more probable in MCI, AD, ALS, and cognitively impaired CVD groups compared to controls (all P < 0.05). The p-tau217 to NfL ratio discriminated ALS from AD with an ROC-AUC of 0.92 (95% CI 0.85-0.97) compared to p-tau217 alone at 0.65 (95% CI 0.52-0.76). No ALS clinical or longitudinal association survived correction for multiple comparisons. Elevated p-tau217 and inferred amyloid-{beta} positivity in ALS provide further evidence that the assay signal is not necessarily specific for AD pathology. However, the use of p-tau217 in combination with NfL provides improved discriminatory power between ALS and AD, supporting the use of plasma biomarker combinations rather than sole reliance on individual plasma biomarkers. Inferred amyloid-{beta} positivity in cognitively impaired CVD may indicate AD and/or cerebral amyloid angiopathy co-pathology. Currently available plasma biomarkers should therefore be used as diagnostic complements and interpreted within clinical context rather than as standalone molecular diagnoses.

papers.title: Computational Modeling of the Acoustic Radiation Force and Viscoelastic Displacement for Transcranial Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation
papers.abstract: ObjectiveIn transcranial ultrasound neuromodulation (TUS), simulations of the harmonic pressure are often used for treatment planning. However, other mechanisms of energy transfer, such as acoustic radiation force (ARF) and the resulting tissue displacement, are reported less frequently. Furthermore, there is limited guidance on how these mechanisms should be simulated. This study evaluates the numerical convergence and accuracy of different ARF formulations and investigates the simulation of ultrasound-induced tissue displacement in the context of TUS. ApproachTwo simulations steps are used in k-Wave to first simulate the first order acoustic pressure and velocity fields. Subsequently, these fields are used to calculate the ARF using the momentum-flux density tensor, Reynolds stress force, and attenuation force formulations. The ARF is then applied as input for a second viscoelastic simulation to estimate the tissue displacement induced by the ultrasound field. Numerical accuracy and convergence are quantified as functions of the various numerical choices and hyperparameters in the solvers. Main resultsAmong the investigated formulations, the attenuation-force approach proved to be the most robust and the least susceptible to numerical errors across variable medium types and transducer geometries. Within the parameter space relevant to TUS, it is a valid approximation of the momentum flux density tensor formulation. Similar tissue displacement distributions are found across the different ARF formulations. However, the accuracy of the displacement simulation decreases with increasing pulse duration. Finally, recommendations are formulated on the ARF calculation method and on the numerical hyperparameters for ARF and displacement simulations. SignificanceThis study offers guidelines for calculating the ARF and simulating tissue displacement. The proposed framework enables a more comprehensive characterization of ultrasound-mediated energy transfer in TUS.

papers.title: A multi-scale cell-type resolved map of trans-regulatory architecture in the aging human brain
papers.abstract: Mapping genetic effects on distal genes and regulatory programs is essential for understanding how genetic variation influences complex diseases; yet trans-QTL discovery remains limited by weak effect sizes, extensive multiple testing and poor reproducibility. Here, we introduce TransMap, a generalizable computational framework that combines multi-scale trans-QTL mapping with multi-phenotype genetic colocalization to improve the discovery and interpretation of distal regulatory variants. Beyond individual trans-eGenes, TransMap constructs local co-regulatory program phenotypes that account for background expression variation to improve the detection of weak, coordinated distal genetic effects. Across a broad range of simulation settings, TransMap achieved 9.2-36.7% higher trans-QTL discovery power than existing methods while maintaining well-controlled type I error rates. We applied TransMap to bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiles from the aging human brain in the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD), further integrating proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic biomarker measurements (average N=476 donors). Genome-wide fine-mapping of TransMap single-gene and program-level QTL yielded variant annotations with 2.75-2.88x heritability enrichment across 57 complex diseases and traits (average N=307K), with complementary heritability information captured across regulatory scales. Multi-phenotype colocalization identified 49,532 trans-regulatory events supported by shared genetic signals with cis-eQTL or biomarker-QTL, including 1,825 candidate cis-trans-biomarker regulatory configurations. TransMap further revealed an asymmetric cross-cell-type regulatory architecture in which neuronal cis-regulatory signals preferentially associate with coordinated glial trans-regulatory responses, supported by co-culture experiments and spatial transcriptomics. Alzheimers disease (AD) GWAS-prioritized colocalization identified trans-regulatory associations in 115 AD-associated loci, including a KNOP1 cis-eQTL associated in trans with a microglial regulatory program containing MS4A4E, with additional support from statistical mediation analysis. TransMap provides a multi-scale, cell-type-resolved atlas of trans-regulatory variation and a generalizable framework for elucidating the regulatory architecture of complex diseases.

papers.title: Music-Synchronized Gamma Light Stimulation Strengthens Theta-Gamma Coupling in Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment: Results from a Randomized Feasibility Trial
papers.abstract: Noninvasive clinical innovations for restoring gamma activity via sound and light stimulation have the potential to improve memory and cognitive abilities in Alzheimers disease. We assessed whether pairing music with theta- and gamma-band light changes memory-supporting neural dynamics, and whether those changes track cognition. In an ongoing randomized feasibility trial, 38 older adults with cognitive impairment completed eight weeks of an audiovisual intervention. The treatment group (n = 19) listened to self-selected music while viewing light stimulation that consisted of a 39-Hz gamma-band signal modulated by delta- and theta-band musical rhythms. The control group (n = 19) listened to podcasts while viewing synchronized lights without the gamma frequency (delta-band only). Before and after the 8-week intervention, participants completed a face-name association task and the Alzheimers Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive (ADAS-Cog). Individuals in the treatment group showed significant improvements on a face-name association task and the ADAS-Cog. Cluster-based permutation testing showed a larger increase in phase-amplitude coupling between acoustic theta phase and frontal EEG gamma amplitude in the treatment group compared to the control group. Across participants, increases in stimulus-driven theta to EEG-gamma phase-amplitude coupling were associated with improvements in memory. These preliminary results suggest that theta-gamma stimulation delivered through music and lights strengthens cross-frequency coupling, and may correspondingly strengthen associative memory.

papers.title: Cognitive Performance in Prodromal Neuronal α Synuclein Disease
papers.abstract: ImportanceCognitive abnormalities may emerge during prodromal neuronal -synuclein disease (NSD), but their domain specificity and longitudinal course are uncertain. ObjectiveTo characterize baseline cognition and longitudinal change in prodromal NSD compared with healthy controls, NSD-negative genetic carriers, and sporadic Parkinson disease (PD). DesignLongitudinal cohort study using Parkinsons Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI) data, with first visits from July 2010 through April 2026 and up to 4 years of follow-up. SettingMulticenter cohort. ParticipantsHealthy controls (HC; n=244), GBA1 or LRRK2 nonmanifesting carriers without NSD (n=323), prodromal NSD participants recruited through hyposmia or isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder cohorts (n=1640), and sporadic PD (n=824). ExposuresNSD status and clinical cohort. Main Outcomes and MeasuresCognitive summary scores for verbal memory, executive function, processing speed, language, and visuospatial function, and PPMI-defined mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Models adjusted for age, sex, education, and APOE {varepsilon}4 status. ResultsAmong 3031 participants (mean [SD] age, 66.6 [7.0] years; 1322 female [43.6%]), prodromal NSD participants had lower baseline verbal-memory performance than HC (adjusted difference, -0.20 SD; 95% CI, -0.34 to -0.07; adjusted P = .007); NSD-negative genetic carriers did not differ from HC. No other cognitive domain was lower than HC at baseline or longitudinally. In the primary age-adjusted analysis, verbal-memory trajectory differed from HC over 4 years (P = .009), whereas in a smaller age-matched sensitivity subset through year 3, it did not (P = .62); the baseline difference persisted (adjusted difference, -0.28 SD; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.10; P = .003). Adjusted MCI probability increased from 10.2% to 15.1% in prodromal NSD, compared with 8.4% to 5.0% in HC and 13.4% to 17.7% in PD. The increase was greater than in HC (ratio of annual odds ratios, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.58; adjusted P = .04) but not PD (P = .62). Conclusions and RelevanceProdromal NSD was associated with modestly lower verbal memory and increasing MCI probability relative to HC, without lower performance in other cognitive domains. The baseline verbal-memory difference was robust, whereas the longitudinal trajectory finding was not reproduced in the smaller age-matched sensitivity subset. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSWhat cognitive differences characterize prodromal neuronal -synuclein disease, and how do they change over time? FindingsIn this longitudinal cohort study of 3031 participants, prodromal neuronal -synuclein disease was associated with lower verbal memory at baseline than healthy controls, while other cognitive domains were not lower. In the primary age-adjusted analysis, the verbal-memory trajectory differed from healthy controls over 4 years; in a smaller age-matched sensitivity subset through year 3, it did not differ significantly. MeaningCognitive involvement in prodromal neuronal -synuclein disease may be detectable as a modest verbal-memory signal, while longitudinal changes require confirmation.

papers.title: Longitudinal Participation and Cognitive Score Interpretation in the J-TRC Webstudy
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTIONWeb-based registries support remote cognitive assessment for Alzheimers disease research, but participant-driven reassessment raises questions about long-term data yield and interpretation of repeated scores. We evaluated data contribution, selective observation, and retest-dependent estimates of cognitive change in the Japanese Trial-Ready Cohort (J-TRC) Webstudy. METHODSWe analyzed over six years of J-TRC Webstudy data (launched October 2019; registrations through March 31, 2025; assessments through May 31, 2026). We examined data contribution, inactivity, reactivation, score-associated observation, first-exposure contrasts, and sensitivity to retest models and estimators. RESULTSAmong 14,912 registered accounts, 10,863 participants were eligible; 10,645 (98.0%) completed the Cognitive Function Instrument (CFI), 6,419 (59.1%) completed Cogstate, and 5,792 (53.3%) contributed assessments on multiple days. Among those with sufficient opportunity, 19.4% and 14.1% contributed data at or beyond three and five years. After 365 days without assessment, the estimated probability of resuming within two years was 7.2%. Worse prior cognitive scores were associated with lower odds of subsequent assessment (adjusted odds ratios per standard deviation: CFI, 0.952; Cogstate, 0.845). By assessment 12, returnee changes were +0.43 and +1.14 favorable baseline standard deviations (CFI, Cogstate), versus -0.06 and +0.08 in first-exposure contrasts. Marginal CFI time estimates differed under categorical versus flexible retest adjustment (+0.080 versus -0.227 standard deviations/year). DISCUSSIONHigh initial completion was accompanied by limited long-term data contribution. Subsequent assessment was associated with prior scores, and estimated time trends varied by retest model. Reporting assessment histories and testing model sensitivity are important for interpreting repeated online cognitive scores.
